en: The Kṛṣṇopaniṣad. Homage to the venerable gurus. Hariḥ Oṃ.
I bow to that Rāma who, having assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa and attained universal selfhood through his divine play, gratified the multitude of silent sages. || 1 ||
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones.
With firm limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.
May Indra, of far-reaching fame, grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya Ariṣṭanemi grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being.
Oṃ! Peace! Peace! Peace!
Now begins the first section.

Hari Oṃ! Having beheld Śrī Mahāviṣṇu, Rāmacandra, whose characteristics are existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who was beautiful in every limb, the forest-dwelling sages were struck with wonder.
They said to him, "Indeed, your incarnations are counted as beyond reproach; we wish to embrace you."

In another birth, during the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, you shall become gopīs and embrace me; as for those other incarnations, they are indeed gopas and not women—do not make them so. By touching my limbs here, you must maintain mutual union with me, for I am your eternal toucher.
We take refuge in the lineage of the incarnations. || 1 ||
Having heard the words of Rudra and the others, the Blessed One himself spoke:
"I shall perform the piercing of my own limbs; I carry out your request."
All those gods were delighted, saying, "Now we have accomplished our purpose;
he who is Nanda is supreme bliss, and Yaśodā is the abode of liberation."
That Māyā is said to be threefold—Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa. It is declared that the Sāttvika form resides in Rudra, and the Rājasa form resides in Brahmā, the devotee.
The dark (tāmasī) illusion among the factions of the Daityas is indeed said to be threefold;
however, the Vaiṣṇavī Māyā is truly unconquerable, and it was formerly mastered by means of recitation (japya).
Devakī is that daughter of Brahmā who is praised by the Vedas;
Vasudeva is the Nigama, which is the meaning of the Vedas; and Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are the two [goals] of the Vedas.
He who constantly offers praise has descended to the surface of the earth,
sporting in the Vṛndāvana forest together with the gopas, gopīs, and the gods.
The cowherd girls are his cows, the *ṛc* verses are his staff, and the lotus-seated Brahmā is his flute.
The blessed Lord Rudra is his bamboo pole, and Indra, together with the gods, is his tip.
Gokula is the Vaikuṇṭha of the forest; the ascetics there are its trees, the Daityas are greed, anger, and the like, and the Kali age has been cast aside.
Hari himself, assuming a cowherd form and manifesting a body of māyā, is difficult to comprehend; the world is deluded by his illusory power.
She is invincible by all the gods; how could the world's illusion belong to that twice-born man by whom Rudra was made into his lineage and who became Dhrstirupa? (11)
The strength and knowledge of the gods were indeed taken away from them in an instant;
Rāma became Śeṣanāga, and Kṛṣṇa became the eternal Brahman itself.
There were sixteen thousand two hundred women;
those Ṛg-verses and Upaniṣads were indeed the female forms of the Brahman. 13.
This wrestler Cāṇūra is hatred; Muṣṭika is envy; Jaya is pride;
Kuvalayāpīḍa is arrogance; the demon Rakṣa is conceit; and Baka is hypocrisy. || 14 ||
Compassion is indeed Rohiṇī, his mother; Satyabhāmā is the Earth.
Aghāsura is great disease, and King Kaṃsa is the Kali age.
Śama, Mitra, Sudāmā, Satya, Akrūra, Uddhava, and Dama;
he who is Śaṅkha is Viṣṇu himself, established in the form of Lakṣmī. (16)
He who was born from the ocean of milk is remembered as Meghaghoṣa;
by him the Ocean of Milk was made into curds in the house of the pot-breaker.
Having become a child as before, he plays in the great ocean;
he remains established there for the sake of destroying his enemies and for the sake of protection. 18.
For the sake of compassion toward all beings, the Lord created that Discus, which has the appearance of Brahman, as the protector of Dharma born of his own self. (19)
The wind born from Jayantī is known as Camara;
it is that Maheśvara who, appearing with the luster of fire, takes the form of a sword.
Kaśyapa is known as the mortar, Aditi is the rope,
and the discus, conch, perfection, and the dot are all upon the head.
Whatever divine forms wise people speak of, they bow down to those divine forms; of this there is no doubt. || 22 ||
The mace is Kālikā herself, the destroyer of all enemies;
the bow is Śārṅga, his own Māyā; and the autumn season is his excellent meal.
The stalk of the lotus, the seed of the universe, was held in his hand as a mere plaything;
[his other forms were] Garuḍa, the banyan tree, Bhāṇḍīra, Sudāmā, and the sage Nārada.
Vṛndā is devotion, action, and intellect, manifesting to all living beings.
Therefore, the All-pervading Lord is neither different from these nor non-different from them; nor indeed is He divided by them.
Everything belonging to the inhabitants of heaven has been brought down to earth in Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus ends the first section.
Now begins the second section.
From Vāsudeva, indeed, there arose the one named Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is the individual soul (jīva).
He desired, "May I create offspring.
From that, he became known as Pradyumna.
From that, Hiraṇyagarbha, named Ahaṅkāra, was born;
from him were born the ten Prajāpatis, beginning with Marīci, as well as Sthāṇu, Dakṣa, Kardama, Priyavrata, Uttānapāda, and Vāyu.
From those two, all beings arise;
from that very remainder, indeed, all beings are produced,
and into that very same [remainder] they dissolve.
He alone, being born in many ways, protects all; he alone, as the son of Kadrū, fashioning the sciences of grammar, astronomy, and so forth,
while being worshipped by many seekers of liberation, [pervades] the entire earth in one place.
Being held like a mustard seed upon the head by all the sages,
and being entreated by them while the thousand peaks of Meru covered his heads, he cast aside the egoism of the great wind.
That very Blessed One, manifesting himself in many ways to the Blessed One, being born in each age with his entire own form, he is that very Saumitri of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
[mastering] all the sciences of archery and all the sciences of missiles in their many varieties.
Being displeased, he struck down all the *rakṣasas* and established the duties of the four social orders (*cāturvarṇya*).
That very Blessed One, at the time of the junction between the ages (*yugasandhi*), resembling an autumnal cloud—
Vāsudeva, the son of Rohiṇī, while expounding all the weapons and sciences such as the mace, sought to eliminate numerous circles of kings and thus cast down the entire burden of the earth.
That very Blessed One, being born in the fourth age (yuga) into a family of Brahmins,
desiring to uphold all the Upanishads, intending to expand all the Dharma-shastras, and seeking to deliver all people across [the ocean of existence].
Making all the Vaiṣṇava dharmas flourish, he utterly uprooted all heresies;
he is this very one who dwells within the world as its inner controller.
He is the self of all;
he alone is to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation;
he alone is the bestower of liberation.
By remembering this, one is liberated from all sins;
by chanting its name, one attains union with Viṣṇu.
One who studies this during the day destroys the sin committed at night.
Studying at night destroys the evil committed during the day.
This is the secret of the Vedas; this is the secret of the Upaniṣads. Studying this, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
He attains peace, he attains purity of mind, he obtains the fruit of all sacred fords—he who knows this is liberated from the bondage of the body; thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the second section.
Hari Om Tatsat.
Om! O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious.
With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with unharmed wheels grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being.
Om! Peace! Peace! Peace!
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇopaniṣad.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who dwells within the Chief Vital Breath (Mukhya-prāṇa), the delighter of the Goddess of Speech (Bhāratī).
